extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers and stand-up comedians (beginners to pros)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing short three-part jokes for stand-up or written comedy, centered on setup, punch, and tag to maximize and sustain laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: establish one wrong assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Should establish ONE wrong assumption the audience makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The setup must create a single, identifiable expectation in the audience that the punch can pivot against. Keep focus on one incorrect inference rather than multiple streams of expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Should be in the present tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using present tense keeps the audience in the moment and makes the misdirection immediate and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: minimal concrete nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Should use the smallest number of concrete nouns possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fewer concrete nouns reduce clutter and limit possible interpretations, making the intended wrong assumption clearer and the pivot sharper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: avoid telegraphing the punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Should NOT contain words that telegraph the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include signals or keywords that hint at the punch; conceal the pivot so the audience fills in the expected continuation themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: force audience to anticipate next sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Should leave the AUDIENCE to fill in the expected next sentence (so you can subvert it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the setup so listeners mentally complete the obvious continuation; the punch then subverts that completion for surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch: pivot on the wrong assumption
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punch must exploit and invert the specific wrong assumption created by the setup, making the shift logically connected yet surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch: pivot word last
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the surprise or pivot word at the end of the line to maximize the timing and impact of the reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch: double-meaning lock (reuse word from setup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Should re-use a word from the setup in a new sense if possible (the "double-meaning lock").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recycling a setup word in a different meaning creates a tight, satisfying connection between setup and punch and strengthens the surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch: don't introduce new latent information
rubrics_metrics.description: Should not introduce information that wasn't latent in the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding facts or elements in the punch that the setup did not already allow for; the joke should feel earned by what's already present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag: same premise, not a new joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A second beat off the SAME premise (not a new joke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags must continue or deepen the original premise rather than launching an unrelated gag; they amplify the existing laugh rather than replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag: usually shorter than the punch
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tags concise so they land quickly and keep momentum; longer tags risk diffusing the laugh or changing the beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag: heighten/contrast/comment on the punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightens, contrasts, or comments on the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tag to extend the laugh by raising stakes, offering a surprising contrast, or providing a witty commentary on the punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag: reuse pivot word
rubrics_metrics.description: A great tag re-uses the punch's pivot word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing the pivot word in the tag reinforces the connection and can produce a compounding comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag functions: extend laugh, show riffing, reframe
rubrics_metrics.description: The tag is what separates a chuckle from sustained laughter, because it (a) extends the laugh, (b) demonstrates the writer can riff, and (c) reframes the punch one more time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective tags serve multiple roles: keep the audience laughing longer, showcase improvisational or writing skill, and provide an additional reframing that deepens the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-tag pattern: stack up to three tags
rubrics_metrics.description: A masterful comic stacks tags 1, 2, 3 — each extending the laugh that's still in the room. Practical limit: 3 tags. After that, you're in a runner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequential tags to keep exploiting the laughing audience; cap at about three tags to avoid turning the bit into a 'runner' (a dragged-out, diminishing-return sequence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance length: under 30 seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: Total time on stage: under 30 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a three-part joke/short bit, keep total stage time brief (under 30s) to maintain pace and audience attention—especially in open-mic or rapid-set contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative tag effectiveness: tag gets >=70% of punch laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: The tag gets at least 70% of the punchline's laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful metric for tag strength: a successful tag should secure roughly seventy percent or more of the laugh magnitude generated by the original punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition: audience still laughing before next bit
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience is still laughing when you start the next bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the next joke while the prior laugh is active to preserve momentum; avoid starting a new bit once the laughter has fully subsided.
